evidence.title: Impact of real-life use of artificial intelligence as support for human reading in a population-based breast cancer screening program with mammography and tomosynthesis
evidence.outcome: cancer detection rate, recall rate, and PPV
evidence.effect: AI support increased CDR by 3.2/‰, PPV by 4%, and recall rate by 0.7% compared to reading without AI.
evidence.quote: Comparing global results (including DM and DBT) of double reading with vs. without AI support, we observed an increase in CDR, PPV, and RR by 3.2/‰ (5.8 vs. 9; p < 0.001), 4% (10.6 vs. 14.6; p < 0.001), and 0.7% (5.4 vs. 6.1; p < 0.001) respectively.
evidence.sample_unit: women (screening examinations; 11,998 AI-supported and 11,998 matched historical controls)

evidence.title: Predicting the Value of Radiology Artificial Intelligence Applications: Large-Scale Predeployment Evaluation of a Portfolio of Models
evidence.outcome: Augmentation metrics (AI-detected radiologist-missed cases) predicting postdeployment perceived value
evidence.effect: Absolute and relative enhanced detection rates ranged 0.03-2.27% and 4.5-60.5%; predicted value categories agreed with postdeployment radiologist survey for 10 of 12 tasks (response rate 43.2%, 54/125).
evidence.quote: Perceived value categories agreed between survey respondents and workgroup predictions for 10 of 12 tasks.

evidence.title: Validation and three years of clinical experience in using an artificial intelligence algorithm as a second read system for prostate cancer diagnosis-real-world experience
evidence.outcome: Pathologist-plus-AI second read vs pathologist alone diagnosis changes (AI Impact)
evidence.effect: 2.9% (128/4385) benign cases and 1.21% (24/1984) GG1 cases revised after AI alerts; overall AI Impact 1.8%, ranging 0.75% to 3.5% per pathologist.
evidence.quote: After review by the pathologist, 0.3% (155/57119) of the benign slides and 2.9% (128/4385) of benign cases required a change of diagnosis.
evidence.sample_unit: cases (122,441 slides) in 3-year deployment; validation 101 cases/1279 slides

evidence.title: Use of natural language processing to identify patients with inflammatory breast cancer across a health-care system
evidence.effect: Of 255 confirmed inflammatory breast cancer cases, 57 (22.4%) were identified solely by the AI pipeline and would have been missed by traditional surveillance.
evidence.quote: Of these confirmed cases, 57 (22.4%) were identified solely through the NLP pipeline and would have been missed through traditional surveillance methods.

evidence.title: Locally calibrated error rates improve interpretability of AI scores and influence radiologist decision-making
evidence.outcome: Locally calibrated FDR and FOR estimated per score threshold from local retrospective mammograms
evidence.effect: FDR and FOR varied from 60.87% and 0.03% at low scores to 99.26% and 0.65% at high scores across 130,712 mammograms.
evidence.quote: FDR and FOR varied substantially across AI score thresholds, ranging from 60.87% and 0.03%, respectively, at the low end of the score distribution to 99.26%% and 0.65% at the high end.

evidence.title: Economic evaluation for medical artificial intelligence: accuracy vs. cost-effectiveness in a diabetic retinopathy screening case
evidence.outcome: Effect of local prevalence on optimal AI operating point and predictive values
evidence.effect: At 4%, 8%, 12% prevalence, best cost-effective AI needed higher sensitivity as prevalence rose; PPV fell (e.g., 0.397 to 0.299 at 8%) while NPV rose; urban vs rural required different sensitivity (96.9% vs 94.7%).
evidence.quote: In health economic settings characterized by higher prevalence and higher WTP levels, the AI necessitated higher sensitivity (paired with lower specificity) to achieve the best cost-effectiveness.
evidence.sample_unit: participants with diabetes (simulated cohort; 1100 sensitivity/specificity scenarios)

evidence.title: Grading of diabetic retinopathy using a pre-segmenting deep learning classification model: Validation of an automated algorithm
evidence.outcome: Predictive values extrapolated to local real-world prevalence versus study enriched prevalence
evidence.effect: At study prevalence 80% NPV for DL was 48%; at real-world prevalence 23.8% NPV was 92% and PPV 57%, showing metrics change substantially at local prevalence.
evidence.quote: Using the real‐world DR prevalence of 23.8% for Funen Island, Denmark (Larsen et al., 2017 ), the PPV were 63%, 64% and 57%, and the NPV was 98% for Models 1 and 2, and 92% for Model 3 (Table 2 ).

evidence.title: A Multianalyte Machine Learning Model to Detect Wrong Blood in Complete Blood Count Tube Errors in a Pediatric Setting
evidence.outcome: positive predictive value at low prevalence
evidence.effect: Estimated PPVs ranged from 0.01 to 0.67 for CBC with Diff and 0.01 to 0.75 for CBC without Diff, depending on threshold.
evidence.quote: Assessment on a downsampled, "low prevalence" validation data set resulted in estimated positive predictive values ranging from 0.01 to 0.67 (CBC with Diff) and 0.01 to 0.75 (CBC without Diff), depending on the probability threshold chosen.

evidence.title: Evaluating the impact of data biases on algorithmic fairness and clinical utility of machine learning models for prolonged opioid use prediction
evidence.outcome: Clinical utility via standardized net benefit across subgroups and thresholds
evidence.effect: Net benefit range shifted from [0.1-0.5] to [0.2-0.6]; opioid-exposed required threshold ~0.5 vs ~0.2 in the general cohort, revealing utility loss not seen in AUROC.
evidence.quote: For example, opioid-exposed patients required a threshold probability of ∼.5 to achieve net benefit from the model, compared to ∼.2 in the general cohort.

evidence.title: Real-world evaluation of an automated EEG spike detection software in a tertiary centre compared to a clinical reference standard
evidence.outcome: Predictive values at local prevalence of IEDs in routine EEGs
evidence.effect: With 53 of 484 records IED-positive, PPV was 19.9% and NPV 96.3%, showing utility differs from pre-selected IED-rich datasets.
evidence.quote: Previous evaluations of machine learning models have reported non-inferiority compared to human experts, but these studies predominantly use small datasets of pre-selected, 'IED rich' records, which are not representative of clinical practice.

evidence.title: Implementing an AI algorithm in the clinical setting: a case study for the accuracy paradox
evidence.outcome: Mismatch between vendor-reported metrics and predictive values at local prevalence
evidence.effect: Local PPV 33% vs manufacturer's 95-98%; false discovery rate 67%; tool perceived inaccurate and removed from practice.
evidence.quote: To mitigate the accuracy paradox, radiologists should be presented with metrics based on a disease prevalence similar to their practice when evaluating and utilizing artificial intelligence tools.
evidence.sample_unit: patients undergoing CTA in the emergency department

evidence.title: Real world clinical experience of using Brainomix e-CTA software in a medium size acute National Health Service Trust
evidence.outcome: Predictive values at local low prevalence of LVO
evidence.effect: With LVO prevalence 9% (n=50), PPV was only 0.5 (0.42-0.58) despite specificity 0.93, showing clinical utility may be overstated.
evidence.quote: We hypothesized that in real world use where prevalence is low, its clinical utility may be overstated.

evidence.title: Real-World Assessment of the Efficacy of Computer-Assisted Diagnosis in Colonoscopy: A Single Institution Cohort Study in Singapore
evidence.outcome: Negative predictive value of adenoma characterization by anatomic region, reflecting local polyp prevalence
evidence.effect: NPV was 80.3% for rectosigmoid lesions vs 54.2% for colonic lesions, attributed to hyperplastic polyp prevalence of 11.4% vs 5.4%. Overall sensitivity 89.4%, specificity 61.7%, NPV 69.8%.
evidence.quote: The negative predictive value for rectosigmoid lesions (80.3%) was notably higher than for colonic lesions (54.2%), attributed to the increased prevalence of hyperplastic rectosigmoid polyps (11.4%) vs other colonic regions (5.4%).

evidence.title: Cross-Cohort Generalizability of Plasma Biomarker Machine Learning Models Reveals Calibration-Driven Degradation in Clinical Utility
evidence.outcome: Predictive values and net benefit under cross-cohort transfer with differing prevalence
evidence.effect: NPV dropped ~19 points under transfer; decision curve analysis showed reduced net clinical benefit; prevalence differences critically affect NPV.
evidence.quote: Calibration instability and prevalence differences critically affect NPV, highlighting the need for cross-cohort validation, calibration assessment, and assay harmonization before clinical implementation.

evidence.title: An autonomous agentic workflow for clinical detection of cognitive concerns using large language models
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity change from balanced refinement dataset to real-world-prevalence validation dataset
evidence.effect: Sensitivity decreased from 0.91 to 0.62 between datasets; F1 for expert-driven workflow 0.81 in validation vs 0.87 in refinement, agentic 0.74 vs 0.93, attributed to prevalence shift.
evidence.quote: Sensitivity decreased from 0.91 to 0.62 between datasets, demonstrating the impact of prevalence shift on generalizability.

evidence.title: Combining Machine Learning Models and Screening to Enhance Suicide Risk Identification for American Indian Patients: Retrospective Cohort Study
evidence.outcome: Predictive values at local prevalence for suicide risk identification
evidence.effect: At 0.4% outcome prevalence, PPVs were low (0.012-0.050) despite reasonable sensitivity/specificity; NPV 0.997-0.999.
evidence.quote: The PPVs we observed (0.012-0.050) reflect the mathematical reality that low prevalence constrains PPV even when sensitivity and specificity are reasonable, a challenge inherent to predicting any rare outcome.

evidence.title: Development and external validation of AI-ECG models in athlete pre-participation screening: Performance, limitations, and clinical implications
evidence.outcome: Predictive values at local screening prevalence versus hospital-based performance
evidence.effect: NPV ~99% but PPV ≤8% at low prevalence (VHD 4.3%, CM 2.7%), showing strong prevalence dependence.
evidence.quote: Threshold analyses showed high negative predictive values (∼99%) but persistently low positive predictive values (≤8%), reflecting limited disease enrichment and strong prevalence dependence.

evidence.title: Clinical transportability, calibration drift, and local updating of a B-mode ultrasound radiomics-clinical prediction model for occult high-volume central lymph node metastasis in cN0 papillary thyroid carcinoma: development, temporal validation, and external validation
evidence.outcome: Predictive values at local prevalence at fixed threshold
evidence.effect: At fixed threshold 0.565, PPV/NPV were 0.792/0.749, 0.877/0.774, 0.769/0.805 and 0.594/0.897 across cohorts, varying with local event rate.

commentary.bottom_line: Ten studies, most of them offline analyses, consistently show that predictive values and clinician-plus-AI performance change substantially when measured at local prevalence, and one deployment study found that local augmentation metrics matched later radiologist-perceived value for 10 of 12 tasks. No study tests whether reporting these metrics leads to better adoption decisions or patient outcomes.

perspectives.view: Of 10 studies, 6 are level 4 offline analyses and none is randomized. Results consistently show predictive values shifting with prevalence, for example NPV rising from 48% to 92% (39425597) and PPV of 19.9% in routine EEGs (41615503). Most studies demonstrate the arithmetic rather than effects on decisions, so indirectness keeps certainty low.

In Spain, AI support raised cancer detection by 3.2 per 1,000 and PPV by 4%, with recall up 0.7% (37975920). That tradeoff became visible only through comparison with local readers. At 0.4% prevalence, suicide-risk PPVs were 0.012 to 0.050 (42114005), which suggests local reporting may reveal false-alarm burdens before deployment.

Local metrics appear feasible to produce from routine data. One site computed calibrated false discovery rates across 130,712 local mammograms (PPR985282). Augmentation metrics from 88,645 examinations agreed with radiologist-perceived value for 10 of 12 tasks, though the survey response rate was 43.2% (41779377). Net benefit analysis showed subgroup threshold shifts that AUROC did not show (41036091).

One emergency department found a local PPV of 33% against a manufacturer-reported 95% to 98% (39741216). Elsewhere, a specificity of 0.93 yielded a PPV of 0.5 at 9% stroke prevalence (39878893). These findings suggest that performance figures supplied at purchase may not transfer, which is consistent with the multi-society radiology statement on reporting predictive values at local prevalence.

The emergency department tool with a local PPV of 33% was removed from practice (39741216). Local evaluation before purchase might have avoided that sunk cost. The augmentation-metric approach (41779377) suggests systems may be able to forecast perceived value before full rollout. None of the supplied studies reports the staff time or data costs of producing local estimates.

A three-year pathology deployment in Puerto Rico found that pathologist-plus-AI review revised 1.8% of diagnoses, with rates of 0.75% to 3.5% per pathologist (38868487). A Chinese simulation found that rural and urban settings required different sensitivity, 94.7% versus 96.9% (38383738). Both suggest that site-level metrics differ, but neither study examined Medicaid or safety-net populations.

In one surveillance program in the United States, 57 of 255 inflammatory breast cancer cases (22.4%) were identified only by the AI pipeline (40493814). Comparisons with local clinicians may show patients what a tool adds to their own care team. Low local PPVs indicate how often patients may face false alarms and follow-up testing.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares health systems that report local metrics with systems that rely on vendor or published metrics. The effect of local reporting on purchasing decisions, clinician trust, and patient outcomes therefore remains untested. Studies also do not report the case volume, staff time, or cost needed to generate stable local estimates, particularly at low prevalence where confidence intervals widen.
commentary.underserved_note: The Puerto Rico pathology deployment focused on a racial and ethnic minority population, and one Chinese simulation modeled rural settings. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Prevalence and case mix may differ in these settings, so metrics reported at the tested sites may not reflect local utility there, and the practice itself has not been evaluated in them.
